text:
German philosophy - Wikipedia
Contents
German philosophy
German philosophy
is
philosophy
in the
German language
or philosophy by
German people
, a part of
German culture
.
It covers figures such as
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
,
Immanuel Kant
,
Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
,
Karl Marx
,
Friedrich Nietzsche
,
Martin Heidegger
,
Gottlob Frege
,
Ludwig Wittgenstein
, the
Vienna Circle
, and the
Frankfurt School
.
German philosophers are central to major philosophical movements such as
rationalism
,
German idealism
,
Romanticism
,
dialectical materialism
,
existentialism
,
phenomenology
,
hermeneutics
,
logical positivism
, and
critical theory
.
[
1
]
[
2
]
[
3
]
German philosophy influenced both contemporary philosophical schools: the
analytic
and
continental
traditions, though naturally most German universities study continental philosophy. Martin Heidegger and Ludwig Wittgenstein are considered two of the most influential philosophers of the 20th century.
Middle ages
While
Saint Ambrose
(c. 339–397) was born in modern-day Germany, German philosophy starts much later.
[
4
]
Medieval philosophy
was often
Christian philosophy
. The first philosophical controversy on German soil happened in the year 848, when
Rabanus Maurus
(
c.
780–856), a student of
Charlemagne
's preferred scholar
Alcuin of York
, responded to
Gottschalk of Orbais
' doctrine of
double predestination
.
[
5
]
Rabanus was deacon at the
Benedictine
Abbey of Fulda
in
Hesse
, and has been called "the first teacher of Germany".
[
6
]
The other center of learning in Germany was
St. Emmeram's
in
Regensburg
.
Otloh of Sankt Emmeram
(c. 1010–c. 1072) and
Manegold of Lautenbach
(c. 1030–c. 1103) were sophisticated defenders of
anti-philosophy
.
[
7
]
By the twelfth century, all the monks at St. Emmeram's were said to be illiterate.
[
4
]
[
8
]
[
a
]
Latin literacy had declined so much that
Notker Labeo
(
c.
950–1022) translated the Roman
Neoplatonist
Boethius
,
Capella
, and some
Aristotle
, inventing the first German philosophical vocabulary.
[
10
]
[
11
]
The few
twelfth-century Renaissance
German philosophers during the
High Middle Ages
begin with
Hugh of Saint Victor
(
c.
1096–1141), who studied at the
abbey of Saint Victor
in Paris, and wrote on Neoplatonic
mystical
philosophy.
[
12
]
[
13
]
Otto of Freising
(
c.
1111–1158) was likely Hugh's student
[
14
]
[
15
]
and introduced to Germans the
new
,
complete
logic of Aristotle
.
[
16
]
Hugh also influenced Italian philosopher
Peter Lombard
, author of the
Sentences
(c. 1150).
[
17
]
[
18
]
Neoplatonist nun and polymath
Hildegard von Bingen
(
c.
1098
–1179) called the "
Sibyl
of the
Rhine
" knew Latin and wrote on theology, cosmology, and natural philosophy.
[
b
]
In works like
Scivias
(1151), she wrote God infused life with
viriditas
.
[
20
]
Aristotle's other works became available from
translators
in
Spain
, one of whom was
Herman the German
. The most eminent German
Scholastic
,
Dominican
friar
Saint Albert the Great
(
c.
1200–1280), taught the
Physics
at Paris and
Cologne
.
[
21
]
[
22
]
[
23
]
He influenced Neoplatonist
Theodoric of Freiberg
(
c.
1250
–
c.
1311
).
[
24
]
The
Italian
Thomas Aquinas
was also Albert's student.
[
25
]
Aristotle translator
William of Moerbeke
(c. 1225–c. 1286) might have also been one.
[
26
]
Aristotelians
with a blend of Neoplatonism like Theodoric were known as Albertists in contrast to the purely Aristotelian
Thomists
.
[
27
]
German Dominicans were usually Albertists, such as
Ulrich
(c. 1225–1277) and
Hugh Ripelin of Strassburg
(c. 1205–c. 1270).
[
28
]
German Thomists included
John of Lichtenberg
,
Heinrich of Lübeck
,
Heinrich of Gorkum
,
Nicholas
and
Thomas of Strassburg
, and
John
and
Gerhard of Sterngassen
.
[
29
]
[
c
]
Meister Eckhart
(
c.
1260
–
c.
1328
), an influential Neoplatonic
mystic
at Cologne, wrote the
Book of Divine Consolation
.
[
31
]
Eckhart combined Theodoric's mysticism with the non-philosophical mysticism found among
beguine
orders, like
Mechthild of Magdeburg
(c. 1207–c. 1282), author of
The Flowing Light of the Godhead
.
[
4
]
[
32
]
[
33
]
Meister Eckhart was posthumously condemned for heresy, and defended by
Henry Suso
(1295–1366).
[
34
]
Eckhart influenced the
Friends of God
and
Brabantine
priest
John of Ruusbroec
,
[
35
]
who influenced the
Brethren of the Common Life
and
Devotio Moderna
proponent
Thomas à Kempis
, author of
The Imitation of Christ
.
[
36
]
Albertist
Berthold of Moosburg
(d. c. 1365) succeeded Eckhart at Cologne.
[
37
]
Johannes Tauler
(c. 1300–1361) held similar views.
[
38
]
Albertist
Heymeric de Campo
(1395–1460) taught at Cologne.
[
39
]
A contemporary Thomist at Cologne was
Lambertus de Monte
(c. 1430–1499).
[
40
]
Thomas of Erfurt
(fl. c. 1300) was the most influential of the Aristotelian so called
modistae
or speculative grammarians active in Northern Europe at the time.
[
41
]
[
d
]
They opposed nominalism and argued for
realism
.
[
42
]
German Renaissance
The
British philosopher
and
Franciscan
William of Ockham
(c. 1287–1347) spent his final years taking refuge with
Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor
at the
Alter Hof
in
Munich
.
[
43
]
[
44
]
Ockham's
nominalism
proved influential in Germany.
[
45
]
The
Schism of 1378
drove many nominalists from France to Germany.
[
4
]
[
45
]
The first university in the
Holy Roman Empire
was the
University of Prague
(1347), modeled after the
University of Paris
, then influenced by Ockhamist
Jean Buridan
.
[
46
]
Buridan's student
Albert of Saxony
(
c.
1320–1390) contributed to logic, and to physics with a
theory of impetus
, a precursor to
inertia
.
[
47
]
He became the first rector at the second, the
University of Vienna
(1365).
[
47
]
Henry of Langenstein
(c. 1325–1397), who with
Henry of Oyta
(c. 1330–1397) followed Albert of Saxony at Vienna, taught Ockham's
conciliar theory
.
[
48
]
[
49
]
Albert of Saxony's student
Marsilius of Inghen
(c. 1340–1396) became first rector at the third, the
University of Heidelberg
(1386).
[
50
]
The Dominican
Cologne
was converted into a
studium generale
(c. 1388) and was the fourth.
[
4
]
The most notable German Ockhamist was
Gabriel Biel
(
c.
1420–1495), first professor of theology at the
University of Tübingen
in 1484.
[
51
]
[
e
]
Nicholas of Cusa
(1401–1464) and
Dutch philosopher
Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam
(c. 1466–1536) were two major figures of
Northern Renaissance
(and
German Renaissance
)
humanism
, along with
Conrad Celtis
(1459–1508).
[
53
]
Cusa was influenced by
negative theology
and a student of Heymeric de Campo.
[
54
]
He was a mystic who believed in the
coincidentia oppositorum
, suggesting Cusa was a
dialetheist
, denying the
law of non-contradiction
.
[
55
]
Cusa's
De Docta Ignorantia
(
Of Learned Ignorance
) (1440) maintains the finite, human mind cannot fully know the divine, infinite mind ('the Maximum'), but can nonetheless attain "learned ignorance".
[
37
]
Johannes Gutenberg
(1406–1468) invented the
printing press
. The creation of the
Gutenberg Bible
(c. 1455) marked the start of the
Gutenberg Revolution
and the age of the printed book in the
Western world
.
[
56
]
Desiderius Erasmus was a scholar of medieval Christianity and a
skeptic
.
[
57
]
His contemporaries charged him with “laying the egg that Luther hatched.”
[
58
]
Erasmus is best known for works like
The Praise of Folly
(1511) and
Handbook of a Christian Knight
(1501).
[
59
]
Another humanist was
Johann Heynlin
(c. 1425–1496), a
realist
opponent of nominalism.
[
60
]
Johann Reuchlin
(1455–1522) was another.
[
61
]
He advocated teaching Greek and Hebrew, and wrote on the
Jewish mysticism
of
Kabbalah
in
De Arte Cabalistica
(1517).
[
62
]
Martin Luther
(1483–1546), a
moral theology
professor at the
University of Wittenberg
, started the
Reformation
.
Luther's translation of the Bible
into German made it vastly more accessible to the laity, having a wide impact on both the Church and German culture. Luther sparked an international debate on
indulgences
and other Church practices in works like
Ninety-five Theses
(1517). According to
Philip Melanchthon
(1497–1560), they were posted on the door of
All Saints' Church, Wittenberg
.
[
63
]
Luther is considered one of the most influential figures in
Western
and
Christian history
.
[
64
]
[
65
]
Protestantism
and
Lutheranism
held
salvation
was achieved by faith alone (
sola fide
) and through God alone (
monergism
). While Luther praised reason as "the best and something divine,"
[
66
]
he saw it as inadequate in achieving knowledge of God, calling reason "the
Devil
's
harlot
".
[
67
]
Erasmus argued against Luther in
On Free Will
(1524), defending
free will
and
synergism
. Led by Erasmus's former assistant
Œcolampadius
(1482–1531),
Basel
adopted the Reformation in 1529, when elected Catholic councilmen were deposed.
[
68
]
Erasmus left by ship to the Catholic university town
Freiburg im Breisgau
, to receive the protection of his former student,
Archduke Ferdinand of Austria
.
[
69
]
Erasmus influenced German
Anabaptists
such as
Balthasar Hubmaier
.
[
70
]
The doctrines of French logician, education reformer, and Protestant convert
Petrus Ramus
known as
Ramism
influenced
Freigius
(1543–1583),
Caspar Olevian
(1536–1587) and
Johannes Piscator
(1536–1625).
[
71
]
Ramist and follower of Melanchthon
Rudolph Goclenius
(1547– 1628) taught
Otto Casmann
(1562– 1607), a humanist, Protestant convert who attempted
Mosaic physics
.
[
72
]
Johannes Trithemius
(1462–1516) was a humanist and mystic
hermeticist
who taught
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
(1486–1535) and
Paracelsus
(1493–1541).
[
73
]
[
74
]
The Albertists and Erasmus also influenced Nettesheim.
[
75
]
His
Three Books of Occult Philosophy
(1533) was widely influential among esotericists, and condemned as
heretical
by the inquisitor of Cologne.
[
76
]
His
skepticism
also proved influential, found in
On the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Arts and Sciences: An Invective Declamation
(1530).
[
77
]
Paracelsus was an
alchemist
and pioneer of the
Medical Renaissance
called the "father of
toxicology
".
[
78
]
In addition to Aristotle's four
classical elements
(
earth
,
water
,
air
, and
fire
), Paracelsus added three principles or
tria prima
(
sulphur
,
mercury
, and
salt
). Paracelsus thought the
tria prima
contained the poisons contributing to all diseases.
[
79
]
Gerhard Dorn
,
Oswald Croll
,
Andreas Libavius
,
Heinrich Khunrath
, and
Valentin Weigel
helped popularize his work.
[
80
]
[
81
]
Valentin Weigel (1533–1588) also followed religious radicals
Thomas Müntzer
,
Andreas Bodenstein von Karlstadt
,
Sebastian Franck
, and
Caspar Schwenckfeldt
, who believed Christ could be known internally, without reading.
[
82
]
Pietist
predecessor
Johann Arndt
(1555–1621) and Pietist
Gottfried Arnold
(1666–1714) helped spread Valentin Weigel's ideas.
[
83
]
17th century
Melanchthon taught the
Wittenberg interpretation
of
Copernicus
and influenced the Protestant mathematicians
[
f
]
who introduced Copernicus to natural philosopher
Johannes Kepler
(1571–1630). Kepler was a key figure in the
Scientific
and
Copernican Revolution
,
[
84
]
known for advancing
heliocentrism
and his
laws of planetary motion
,
[
85
]
found in such books as
Astronomia nova
,
Harmonice Mundi
, and
Epitome Astronomiae Copernicanae
.
In
Mysterium Cosmographicum
(1596) Kepler proposed the distance relationships between the planets could be understood by the five
Platonic solids
, showing the influence of Plato's
Timaeus
.
[
86
]
Kepler also wrote the
Rudolphine Tables
(1627), based on the data and measurements of Dane
Tycho Brahe
.
[
87
]
Lutheran mystic philosopher
Jakob Böhme
(1575–1624) was influenced by Valentin Weigel and wrote
The Way to Christ
(1624). Böhme founded
Christian theosophy
and
Behmenism
.
[
g
]
A key concept for Böhme is the
Ungrund
, the un-
grounded
, primeval
abyss
prior to the
creation of the world
, but that is also a
will
and pure
freedom
.
[
90
]
Piscator's grandson
Tobias Andreae
,
Johannes Clauberg
,
Johann Eberhard Schweling
, and
Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus
defended
Cartesianism
, the views of French "father of
modern philosophy
"
René Descartes
(1596–1650).
[
91
]
[
92
]
Princess Elizabeth of Bohemia
(1618–1680) posed the interaction problem for
substance dualism
to Descartes.
[
93
]
Lutheran philosopher and
mathematician
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
(1646–1716) wrote primarily in
Latin
and
French
, such as the
Discourse on Metaphysics
(1686) and
Nouveaux Essais
(1689). Leibniz, along with Descartes and
Baruch Spinoza
(1632–1677), was one of the three great advocates of
rationalism
, the
epistemological
view that "regards
reason
as the chief source and test of knowledge,"
[
94
]
[
95
]
rather than
empirical evidence
. Leibniz believed necessary truths were based on the
law of non-contradiction
, and
contingent
truths on the
principle of sufficient reason
.
[
96
]
He anticipated modern
logic
and
analytic philosophy
with his wish for a universal language (
characterista universalis
) and logical calculus (
calculus ratiocenator
),
[
97
]
but his philosophy also looks back to the scholastic tradition.
[
98
]
Leibniz expounded an
idealist
theory of
monads
in works like
Monadologie
(1714). Monads are the ultimate elements composing the
universe
, and can be compared to the corpuscles of Descartes's
mechanical philosophy
; except for Descartes objects are merely
extended
in space, while Leibniz agreed with the scholastics that objects have
substantial forms
and
entelechy
.
[
99
]
[
100
]
[
101
]
Monads are centers of
force
; while
space
,
matter
, and
motion
are merely phenomenal or
relational
.
[
99
]
Monads additionally have the following properties: they are
simple
(having no parts)
substances
, eternal, individual, subject to their own laws, un-interacting ("windowless"), and seem to interact causally due to God's
pre-established harmony
(a historically important example of
panpsychism
).
[
99
]
Leibniz is also noted for his optimism – his
Théodicée
(1710) tries to
resolve
the
problem of evil
by claiming this is the
best of all possible worlds
.
[
102
]
This is because it was created by an all powerful and all knowing God, who would not choose to create an imperfect world if a better world could be known to him or possible to exist. Any flaws in this world must exist in every possible world, because otherwise God would have chosen to create the world without them.
[
102
]
A heavy influence on the
Enlightenment
was British natural philosopher
Sir Isaac Newton
(1643–1727) and his philosophy of
Newtonianism
. Influenced by Kepler, Newton published
Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica
(1686) and his
laws of motion
, introducing
classical mechanics
to
physics
.
[
103
]
Leibniz and Newton
disputed
who had invented
calculus
.
[
104
]
Leibniz and Newton also disagreed on space.
[
105
]
Occasionalists
think only God causes things. The occasionalists were Leibniz teacher
Erhard Weigel
(1625–1699), and Descartes and Leibniz critic
Johann Sturm
(1635–1703).
[
106
]
Erhard Weigel was also a teacher of
Samuel von Pufendorf
(1632–1694). Pufendorf supported
religious tolerance
following the
Thirty Years War
(1618–1648), and authored
On the Duty of Man and Citizen
(1673).
[
107
]
18th century
Pufendorf's follower was
Christian Thomasius
(1655–1728). Thomasius lecturing in German is commonly seen as the start of the
German Enlightenment
(
Aufklärung
).
[
108
]
This also spread to the
Swiss Enlightenment
.
[
h
]
The most eminent German philosopher between Leibniz and Kant was
Christian Wolff
(1679–1754). Leibniz and Wolff are often grouped together as “Leibnizian-Wolffian philosophy”.
[
109
]
Wolff's rationalism was criticized by the
Pietists
at the
University of Halle
like
Philipp Spener
(1635–1705) and
August Hermann Francke
(1663–1727).
[
109
]
Wolff studied what he called both theoretical and practical philosophy, which includes
economics
and
public administration
. His main achievement was an
oeuvre
studying almost every scholarly subject of his time, displayed according to his logical method, which perhaps represents the peak of German Enlightenment
rationality
.
[
109
]
Wolff was a pioneer of German language scholarship, replacing Latin terminology with German words, but he also wrote in Latin for an international audience.
[
110
]
[
111
]
Wolff and his disciple at Tübingen, logician
Gottfried Ploucquet
(1716–1790), were originally occasionalists, but eventually abandoned the view.
[
106
]
Georg Bernhard Bilfinger
(1693–1750) and
Israel Gottlieb Canz
(1690–1753) also followed Wolff at Tübingen.
[
112
]
August Friedrich Bök
(1739–1815) was an influential student of Ploucquet.
[
113
]
Wolff influenced German Enlightenment natural philosophy pioneer
Tobias Mayer
(1723–1762).
[
114
]
[
115
]
Alsatian polymath
Johann Heinrich Lambert
(1728–1777) further developed the logic of Ploucquet, and the natural philosophy of Mayer.
[
116
]
After Mayer's death,
Abraham Gotthelf Kästner
(1719–1800) was director of the Observatory at
Göttingen
.
[
117
]
Kästner taught philosopher and physicist
Georg Christoph Lichtenberg
(1742–1799).
[
118
]
Art theorists
Alexander Gottlieb Baumgarten
(1714–1762) and
Georg Friedrich Meier
(1718–1777) were students of Wolff. Baumgarten coined the term
aesthetics
, and Meier was the teacher of
Aufklärer
Thomas Abbt
(1738–1766).
[
119
]
Moses Mendelssohn
(1729–1786) of the
Haskalah
, or 'Jewish Enlightenment', wrote
Phaedon
(1767), a defense of immortality, after the death of Thomas Abbt. One scholar describes Mendelssohn as “the last great representative of the Leibniz-Wolffian school”.
[
120
]
[
121
]
[
i
]
Mendelssohn influenced
Salomon Maimon
(1753–1800).
[
122
]
Abbt admired
Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
(1729–1781), who embraced the Enlightenment and
religious tolerance
, for instance in his play
Nathan the Wise
(1779), written as a tribute Mendelssohn.
[
123
]
Lessing said there was an "ugly, broad ditch" between the "accidental truths of history" and "the necessary truths of reason".
[
124
]
Lessing published the work of deist and rationalist
Hermann Samuel Reimarus
(1694–1768) anonymously as the
Wolfenbüttel
Fragmente
.
[
125
]
A friend of Lessing and Mendelssohn was
Christoph Friedrich Nicolai
(1733–1811), who influenced popular philosopher
Johann August Eberhard
(1739–1809).
[
126
]
[
127
]
As well as Kant, Lambert, Eberhard, and
Johannes Nikolaus Tetens
(1736–1807) were early phenomenologists.
[
128
]
[
129
]
[
130
]
Tetens has been called the "German
Locke
" and was influenced by
Scottish common sense realism
.
[
131
]
Königsberg University
professor
Immanuel Kant
(1724–1804) studied under Wolffian
Martin Knutzen
(1713–1751).
[
132
]
Kant published his elaborate philosophy of
transcendental idealism
in the
Critique of Pure Reason
(1781). Since its publication, Kant has been considered one of the greatest influences in all of western philosophy. Kant saw himself engaged in a "Copernican Revolution", shifting one's outlook into the mind rather than out to the world.
[
133
]
Kant was regarded as the "destroyer" of (scholastic)
metaphysics
ever since he was called the "all-destroying Kant" by Mendelssohn.
[
134
]
Kant distinguished between
analytic
truths stipulated by definition, and synthetic truths about the world; as well as between knowledge obtained prior to experience or
a priori
, and after experience, or
a posteriori
.
[
133
]
Kant attempted to determine what can be known about the world, through the use of reason independent of all experience, which Kant called the
synthetic a priori
. Briefly, he concluded knowledge is had through experience, but what can be known is limited by how the mind can think: if we can only comprehend things in terms of, for example, cause and effect, then we can only know causes and effects. It follows one can know the form of all possible experience in the apparent,
phenomenal
world; but nothing else, one can never know the
noumenal
world as it really is, the "
thing-in-itself
" absent a standpoint, and therefore one can never know the world in its entirety.
[
135
]
Kant was a Pietist who sought the limits of knowledge “in order to make room for faith”. Kant also published the
Prolegomena
(1783), the
Critique of Practical Reason
(1788), and the
Critique of Judgment
(1790). The
Critique of Practical Reason
has Kant's
deontological
ethics, with the
categorical imperative
; and a
moral argument
for God, free will, and the immortality of the soul.
[
136
]
There was also
Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
(1785) and
The Metaphysics of Morals
(1797). The
Critique of Judgment
contains Kant's
aesthetics
, including his views on the beautiful and the
sublime
. Kant considered disinterest to be a key part of the judgement of
taste
.
[
137
]
Knutzen also introduced Kant to Newtonianism.
[
132
]
Kant was a champion of the
Enlightenment
